content.title: ESPN Unlimited’s First 6 Months: What We’ve Learned
content.text: ESPN’s August direct-to-consumer launch could hardly have been more hyped. In 2024, Disney CEO Bob Iger said the coming offering “will be the best product the consumer has ever seen in sports.” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro described ESPN’s app updates as “one of the biggest days at ESPN, if not the biggest.” At the same time, those atop the company made clear that the introduction of ESPN Select and ESPN Unlimited were the beginning of something rather than a finish line. One football season into the new effort, here’s what we’ve learned about ESPN’s strategy—and where it’s headed next. ESPN+ here to stay, with new role Before ESPN Unlimited, there was ESPN+, a key stepping stone for the network’s digital ambitions. ESPN+ is no longer the company’s only option for delivering games directly to cord-cutters, which is why that platform now carries less programming than it did a year ago. NWSL fans will be the next to notice that change. In 2025, all 20 ESPN games were available on Plus. This year, none will be. ESPN says that properties typically carried by its linear networks will no longer be on ESPN+; you’ll need ESPN Unlimited access to stream those. However, that doesn’t mean ESPN+ is going away. That service is now being treated like another channel in ESPN’s arsenal, with a series of rights associated with it. PGA Tour Live coverage, NHL out-of-market games, international soccer and smaller college events will continue to live on ESPN+, which is available as part of the overall ESPN Unlimited plan ($30 per month or $300 per year) or the more targeted $13/month ESPN Select offering. On Tuesday, ESPN+ will carry more than 100 events, from NCAA baseball and NBA G League action to Big 12 swimming and diving championships and Jai alai. That said, ESPN hopes to convince many of its roughly 25 million existing ESPN+ subscribers that value awaits them in the larger ESPN package, assuming they aren’t already cable buyers. “You’ll see us implement strategies that sort of tap into the Select audience that exists there to try to incentivize them to see what else is going on on ESPN Unlimited,” ESPN SVP for direct-to-consumer John Lasker said on the Sporticast podcast. Over ESPN Unlimited’s first month, Antenna Data estimates roughly 2.1 million signed up for either ESPN Select (43%) or ESPN Unlimited (57%), not including those who signed up with their cable logins. The company has not released recent subscriber numbers for those services. Roughly 60 million TV subscribers have access to ESPN, down from its peak of roughly 100 million in 2011. Why Comcast, YouTube TV subscribers are still waiting Existing cable subscribers are among the biggest beneficiaries of ESPN’s new streaming schema. In a series of distribution deals, the network has pushed to get ESPN Unlimited access included with standard TV plans, giving customers streaming-only content (including ESPN+ fare) at no extra cost. However, it has taken longer than many customers have wanted to receive that bounty. Comcast integration is expected in a matter of days or weeks, while YouTube TV subscribers might not get access to ESPN Unlimited until closer to the fall. Those delays have complicated ESPN’s messaging around who receives its digital benefits, and left some fans fuming that they are essentially forced to pay twice to watch certain events. “We’re really anxious to serve these sports fans, especially these sports fans that are paying for ESPN through these [TV distributors],” Lasker said. “It does pain us to have some of these gaps in existence … We are ready to get them lit up once YouTube TV and Comcast are ready.” Why the delay? ESPN built a new form of authentication to go with its redeveloped apps. While TV Everywhere technology previously sufficed, the new system gives ESPN more information about who is viewing content, allowing for a more tailored experience—and likely tighter platform control. ESPN Unlimited’s exclusive strategy ESPN has made some of its content exclusive to ESPN Unlimited, with WWE events at the top of the list. Alternate presentations of big events such as Spanish-language coverage and secondary camera views are also locked to the service. It remains to be seen just how aggressive ESPN will be in gating certain content to its digital product, versus using Unlimited as an umbrella package for content available elsewhere. “What we’re trying to do is trying to reinforce the value of an ESPN subscription,” Lasker said. “It’s less about forcing people to have to buy ESPN Unlimited direct-to-consumer. What we’re trying to build is more value into the overall ESPN proposition, no matter how you subscribe. … [New events rights] might not fit on the ESPN linear television networks, but that shouldn’t prevent us from providing value to that ESPN Unlimited subscriber, and that is the anchor tenet.” To date, the biggest brouhaha over Unlimited-only content might have come during the Australian Open, when top courts could only be viewed by Unlimited subscribers outside of linear coverage, while ESPN+ retained coverage of lesser matches, in a change from previous years. Getting used to the blame game With each new programming announcement, some number of fans now seem to expect the worst from ESPN, whether it involves Inside the NBA, NFL RedZone, or MLB.TV. In some cases, Pitaro et al. have no say over the related decisions yet seem to receive a hefty portion of criticism regardless. Partly, that comes with the new territory ESPN has entered. For close to 50 years, the sports broadcaster has invested heavily in games and event coverage that fans accessed via a third-party distributor, most often a cable company. That changed with the introduction of ESPN+ and more significantly with the full embrace of its direct-to-consumer business. ESPN is now responsible not only for the content fans view but in many cases also decisions around who can access what streams, the apps they use to see it, the ads that surround videos and—most significantly—the price many pay for it. That opens the company to new lines of attack and creates a need to recognize how consumers now perceive it. ESPN vs. the other worldwide leaders As an all-in-one streaming service, ESPN is now a big part of parent company Disney’s battle with gigantic competitors Amazon, YouTube and Netflix for viewers’ time and dollars—as well as for sports rights. In parallel to ESPN’s embrace of streaming, those digital entertainment companies are increasingly eager to exclusively carry more games, leading to further fragmentation of where fans watch. As MLB.TV moves into ESPN’s orbit, NBA League Pass has aligned with Amazon Prime Video. Even with the NFL on ESPN’s cap table, the league appears ready to expand its relationships with YouTube and Netflix. ESPN’s bundles with Fox One and NFL+ somewhat simplify the increasingly complicated task of managing the services one needs to watch their favorite sports. But the likelihood of a true all-in-one sports destination—or even a singular hub attached to other services—is now vanishingly small. And that’s before even recognizing the reckoning taking place in local sports streaming. Where ESPN goes from here ESPN remains full-steam ahead on its digital endeavor. Moments of consumer confusion and fan pushback have shown where the service needs to evolve, but they have not slowed the company’s ambition. Tying the MLB.TV signup flow to Unlimited enrollment was the latest proof that ESPN is eager to get as many people as it can inside its new, digital tent. Whether fans stick around through the football-less summer? Whether the ability to sign up for ESPN directly (or bundle it with other Disney products) helps sports media’s superpower withstand continued expected declines among the number of cable buyers? Those are questions for the next six months. (This story has been updated with an additional quote from Lasker in the third paragraph under the second subhead.)
